summary: Gemigliptin is a selective, oral dipeptidyl peptidase-4 (DPP-4) inhibitor used as an adjunct to diet and exercise to improve glycaemic control in adults with type 2 diabetes, as monotherapy or in combination with other antidiabetic agents such as metformin. The usual dose is 50 mg once daily. Like other gliptins, it enhances incretin activity, increasing glucose-dependent insulin secretion and suppressing glucagon, with a low intrinsic risk of hypoglycaemia. Class-level risks include acute pancreatitis, hypersensitivity reactions, severe joint pain, and (rarely) bullous pemphigoid. Gemigliptin is approved in several countries (notably South Korea and other markets) but is NOT FDA-approved; dosing and labelling follow the originator/regional prescribing information.

As monotherapy or in combination with other antidiabetic agents (e.g., metformin) where additional control is needed

moa: Gemigliptin selectively and competitively inhibits dipeptidyl peptidase-4 (DPP-4), the enzyme responsible for the rapid degradation of the incretin hormones GLP-1 and GIP. By inhibiting DPP-4, it prolongs the action of active incretins, which enhances glucose-dependent insulin secretion from pancreatic beta cells and suppresses inappropriate glucagon secretion from alpha cells. The net effect is improved fasting and postprandial glucose control with a low intrinsic risk of hypoglycaemia, because the insulinotropic effect is glucose dependent.

absolute: Known serious hypersensitivity to gemigliptin (anaphylaxis, angioedema)
Type 1 diabetes mellitus and diabetic ketoacidosis (not indicated)
monitor: Signs of pancreatitis (persistent severe abdominal pain)
Liver function if hepatic injury is suspected
Renal function to guide ongoing use

preg: There are insufficient human data on gemigliptin in pregnancy and it is not recommended; poorly controlled diabetes in pregnancy carries maternal and fetal risk, and insulin is the preferred treatment. Discontinue and switch to insulin when pregnancy is planned or confirmed.
lact: It is not known whether gemigliptin is excreted in human milk. Because of insufficient data, use during breastfeeding is not recommended; weigh maternal need against potential infant exposure.
renal: Based on the approval studies, gemigliptin generally does not require dose adjustment across the spectrum of renal impairment, including severe impairment, but local prescribing information should be followed and renal function monitored. (Confirm against the regional/originator label as approvals differ by country.)
hepatic: Use with caution in hepatic impairment; data in moderate-to-severe impairment are limited. Monitor liver function and discontinue if significant hepatic injury occurs without alternative explanation.

major: Insulin - increased risk of hypoglycaemia; consider lowering the insulin dose
Sulfonylureas - additive hypoglycaemia; consider dose reduction
moderate: Other glucose-lowering agents - additive hypoglycaemic effect
ACE inhibitors - possible additive angioedema risk (class effect)
Strong CYP3A4 modulators - may alter gemigliptin exposure (gemigliptin is partly CYP3A4 metabolised); review per label
minor: Beta-blockers - may mask symptoms of hypoglycaemia
interactions.food: May be taken with or without food; food does not meaningfully affect efficacy.
interactions.alcohol: Limit alcohol; it can increase hypoglycaemia risk and worsen glycaemic control.
interactions.diagnostics: Lowers HbA1c and plasma glucose; may raise lipase/amylase if pancreatitis develops and liver enzymes with hepatic injury.

emergency: Anaphylaxis or angioedema with airway compromise
Acute pancreatitis with persistent severe abdominal pain

monitoring: HbA1c every ~3 months and fasting/postprandial glucose to assess control
Renal function before starting and periodically
Liver function if symptoms suggest hepatic injury
Signs and symptoms of pancreatitis and hypersensitivity
counsel: Take one tablet once daily at the same time, with or without food
Stop the medicine and seek care urgently for severe persistent abdominal pain (possible pancreatitis)
Report rash, blistering, or swelling of the face, lips, or throat right away
Recognise and treat low blood sugar, especially if also taking insulin or a sulfonylurea
Keep up diet, exercise, and regular blood-sugar checks; do not stop without medical advice
pk: Glucose-lowering begins within hours; full effect over weeks
Plasma concentration peaks within a few hours of dosing
Long terminal half-life (reported around 17 hours or more), supporting once-daily dosing
Sustained DPP-4 inhibition over 24 hours supports once-daily dosing
Store at controlled room temperature, protected from moisture; keep in original packaging
pearls: Not FDA-approved - gemigliptin is approved in South Korea and several other countries; dosing and labelling follow the originator/regional prescribing information rather than an FDA label
Standard dose is a simple 50 mg once daily; available as a fixed-dose combination with metformin in some markets
Class DPP-4 inhibitor cautions apply: acute pancreatitis, serious hypersensitivity, severe arthralgia, and rare bullous pemphigoid
Low intrinsic hypoglycaemia risk; hypoglycaemia mainly when combined with insulin or a sulfonylurea (reduce the partner dose)
Reported to require little or no renal dose adjustment, but always verify against the local product information
missed: Take the missed dose as soon as remembered on the same day. If it is almost time for the next dose, skip the missed dose and resume the usual once-daily schedule. Do not take two doses at once.
overdose: There is no specific antidote. Manage overdose with supportive care, monitoring of glucose and vital signs, and removal of unabsorbed drug from the gastrointestinal tract where appropriate. Treat hypoglycaemia (more likely if combined with insulin or a sulfonylurea) with glucose. Provide symptomatic and supportive management.
